items.title: Acting Navy Secretary calls suicide attempts on USS Abraham Lincoln ‘suicide mitigations’
items.summary:
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said eight sailors deployed in support of the Iran war attempted suicide. On Tuesday, when pressed by Congress about the declining mental health of deployed sailors, Cao said repeatedly that he saw them as eight “mitigations.”

“You see as eight suicide attempts, I see eight suicide mitigations because of the chaplains we have on board, the deployment resiliency counselors, as well as mental health specialists. Normally, most carrier strike groups, when they deploy, have about one or two suicides. This is well before [Operation] Epic Fury,” Cao said at his Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing Tuesday morning.

At the hearing, Senators pushed Cao to answer questions about quality-of-life issues aboard Navy ships in the Middle East following reports of a lack of nutritious food , plumbing issues , and growing mental health concerns among crews deployed for the ongoing Iran war. 

Military Times first reported in August that two sailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln attempted to jump overboard. In the following weeks, the Navy denied reports of growing mental health issues . Cao said at the time that a “small number of mental health cases were treated with no loss of life,” and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said the reports of the USS Lincoln’s conditions were “completely misrepresented.” 

Two days after pushing back on media reports on conditions aboard the carrier, Navy officials told Task & Purpose that the service was routing additional mental health support to the Carrier Strike Group’s flagship and its supporting vessels.…
items.t: Acting Navy Secretary calls suicide attempts on USS Abraham Lincoln ‘suicide mitigations’

items.title: Deployed troops continue to face unnecessary hurdles while voting
items.summary:
Editor’s note: This report was published in partnership between The Beam, at the Howard Center for Investigative Journalism, and Military Times. 

Master Sgt. Joe Klingbeil wanted to vote in Kentucky’s primary this year. But he was in Germany, where he had volunteered for an assignment as an Army reservist.

Klingbeil registered to vote absentee and asked for a ballot from the Bullitt County Board of Elections. 

He said it never came.

“I never received a mail-in ballot, so I didn’t get to vote in the primaries. I was a little salty about that,” Klingbeil said.

For the 2026 midterm general election, Klingbeil was determined not to let it happen again.

While home in Kentucky on leave in September, he visited the Bullitt County Clerk’s office, where he was told a ballot mailed directly to Germany might not reach him with enough time for him to return it, as the verification process for sending a ballot to Germany would take longer. 

So Klingbeil and his family devised another plan, one designed to track the ballot step by step: It would be mailed to his home in Kentucky, where his son would retrieve the ballot and then mail it to Germany.

“My son got it and immediately went up to the post office and mailed it here to me,” Klingbeil said.

Klingbeil received the ballot Oct. 8. Five days later, he returned the ballot by mail. It had to cross the Atlantic Ocean twice.

Kentucky will not count an overseas military ballot that arrives after polls close on Election Day. It is one of 20 U.S. states with no grace period for an overseas military ballot that was mailed on time…
items.t: Deployed troops continue to face unnecessary hurdles while voting

items.title: Lithuanian president says US troop rotations will continue beyond latest deployment
items.summary:
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said on Monday that U.S. troop rotations in Lithuania would continue beyond the current nine-month deployment, speaking at a ceremony marking the arrival of the latest two U.S. battalions.

Washington first deployed troops to Lithuania, a NATO member bordering Russia and Belarus, in 2014 after Russia’s annexation of Crimea.

Since 2019, it had maintained an armoured battalion of about 1,000 troops on overlapping rotations until the Pentagon paused it earlier this year pending a force posture review.

At the Pabrade military base near the Belarusian border, Nauseda said: “As far as I know, this is not a one-off or a temporary rotation. There is a certain rotation plan extending into the future.”

The U.S. Embassy in Lithuania did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

U.S. Ambassador Kara McDonald, speaking at the same ceremony, did not directly comment on Nauseda’s remarks but described the deployment as “a continuation of rotations” that have taken place since 2014.

“Our purpose here is very clear,” she told reporters. “It is a defensive purpose to project deterrence, to maintain readiness, to stand shoulder to shoulder with our allies. This very much is peace through strength, and this is how we preserve peace.” 

Lithuania has proposed expanding U.S. presence or making it permanent and has offered to cover the costs.

President Donald Trump told reporters last month his administration would “certainly look at” Lithuania’s request.

Lithuania has tripled defense spending since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022…
items.t: Lithuanian president says US troop rotations will continue beyond latest deployment

items.title: She reported her sexual assault. The Marine Corps kicked her out.
items.summary:
Editor’s Note: This article first appeared on The War Horse , an award-winning nonprofit news organization educating the public on military service. Subscribe to their newsletter . 

Marina was training at the Basic School in Quantico, Virginia, when she attended the Marine Corps Ball in November 2023. The annual celebration of the Corps’ birthday was supposed to be a night of revelry and camaraderie. Instead, Marina said, a lieutenant sexually assaulted her at knifepoint.

“It should have been the safest place to be,” she said, “and it was quite literally the most dangerous.”

At Marina’s request, The War Horse is using a pseudonym to protect her identity. Her identity was verified and parts of her account were corroborated through interviews and documents, including a military protective order against her alleged assailant, her retirement and discharge paperwork, and emails from the Marine Corps Special Trial Counsel. The War Horse does not identify survivors of sexual assault without their explicit consent.

Marina initially hesitated to report the assault.

“I had not heard great things in the past [about] the way people were treated after reporting this kind of thing,” she said.

Marina would later say that what her command put her through was worse than the assault itself.

Within about a week, she decided to tell military authorities about the attack. First she filed a “restricted” report, which would allow her to receive support and medical care without automatically triggering an investigation, but ultimately changed her report to an “unrestricted” report, which…
items.t: She reported her sexual assault. The Marine Corps kicked her out.

items.title: Acting Navy Secretary says longer deployments are ‘because’ there aren’t enough ships
items.summary:
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao says sailors are facing longer deployments at sea “because” the service doesn’t have enough ships. 

Cao’s comments came during his confirmation hearing before the Senate Armed Services Committee Tuesday morning. Cao was nominated to the position in September but still needs to be confirmed by the Senate. 

The acting secretary came into the role amid growing concerns from military families and media reports about mounting quality-of-life issues and mental health concerns facing sailors aboard Navy ships deployed to support the Iran war. On Tuesday, Senators pressed Cao for his perspective on issues raised over the last few months, including how the Navy’s ship deployments have averaged closer to a year at sea instead of the Navy’s goal for seven-month deployments .

“The reason why we had to have these extended deployments is really because we only have 286 ships today,” Cao said. “As of today, there’s only 286 ships in the battle force. We need 355, and we’re doing the best we can to get these ships out there as quickly as we can so that sailors are not extended on deployment for a long time away from their families. It causes a lot of maintenance issues for our ships as well.”

The hearing comes a week after Cao reportedly told family members of the USS George H.W. Bush carrier strike group that their sailors would not be coming home before the holidays, and that the deployment might stretch a year. A senior Navy official could not confirm the deployment extension for Task & Purpose, citing operational security.

Sailors assigned to Strike…
items.t: Acting Navy Secretary says longer deployments are ‘because’ there aren’t enough ships

items.title: Civilian staff shortages disrupt essential services at isolated bases, report finds
items.summary:
Hundreds of civilian vacancies have strained baseline services at remote military installations, while federal investigators found the Pentagon had not assessed the effects of its workforce reductions.

At Fort Greely, Alaska, Army officials told federal investigators they planned to close the installation’s dining facility for certain meals because they lacked enough civilian employees to keep it operating full time.

For Sgt. Will Mace, a soldier stationed at Fort Greely, told Military Times that the loss of dining services has complicated meal planning.

“Coordinating meals has been difficult without our dining hall readily available,” Mace said. “Delivery and restaurant options are limited, leaving us having to prepare and plan weeks in advance so our day-to-day isn’t majorly interrupted with a lack of food.”

Civilian workers prepare meals, care for children, manage housing, maintain facilities and provide services that allow military personnel and their families to live and work at installations far from major population centers.

A September Government Accountability Office investigation documented 624 civilian vacancies across a sample of nine remote and isolated installations during fiscal years 2023 through 2025. Those vacancies include 607, approximately 97%, of Morale, Welfare and Recreation positions supporting programs used by service members and their families.

Despite disruptions to critical services, the Pentagon had not assessed how its civilian workforce reductions affected remote installations, according to the GAO.

When essential services lose their…
items.t: Civilian staff shortages disrupt essential services at isolated bases, report finds

items.title: VA wants to stop charging premiums on 16,000 WWII-era veteran life insurance policies
items.summary:
The Department of Veterans Affairs says it can stop charging premiums to thousands of veterans who hold a World War II-era life insurance policy, having collected enough to keep the program going for the lifetime of the remaining policyholders.

The VA proposed the move in a Federal Register notice Tuesday, opening a one-month public comment period prior to making the change official. It pertains to roughly 16,000 veterans who hold National Service Life Insurance, offered as a supplemental life insurance product from 1940 to 1951, and Veterans Reopened Insurance, a narrow extension of the policy to Korean War veterans that was offered in 1965 and 1966.

“The funds that cover these policies are in strong financial position, and VA concludes there are sufficient financial resources to cover future liabilities and cost, while providing adequate margin to guard against adverse experience and allow for the payment of dividends,” officials said in the notice.

Affected policyholders have policies with the codes NSLI–V, VRI–J and VRI–JR, and are now 86 to 101 years old, according to the message. The maximum face value of all the affected policies is $10,000, and they each pay annual dividends of a few hundred dollars with amounts based on the age of the veteran, the longevity of the policy and other factors. Up until now, veterans have been able to apply their dividend to the cost of their premium and get the difference, if applicable, in cash, or purchase paid-up additional insurance.

Ending premium collection will benefit the VA workforce as well as affected veterans,…
items.t: VA wants to stop charging premiums on 16,000 WWII-era veteran life insurance policies

items.title: What We Know About Ukraine’s Strikes That Cut Russia’s Kerch Bridge Road Vehicle Span
items.summary:
The scale and scope of Ukraine’s missile and drone strikes overnight that destroyed a key section of the Kerch Bridge’s road span and caused other damage continue to come into sharper focus. For their part, Russian authorities have pledged to repair the bridge, which serves as a critical link between Russia proper and the occupied Crimean Peninsula, and also has enormous symbolic value. Readers can first get caught up with our initial reporting on the Ukrainian operation.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said that the strikes that finally brought down part of the Kerch Bridge were part of a weeks-long phased operation. He also said this was in retaliation for Russia’s continued strikes on Ukrainian energy and other infrastructure. New waves of strikes on the bridge could still be coming.

A look at the destroyed section of the Kerch Bridge road span. via X 

“Grateful to the Security Service of Ukraine, all units of Ukraine’s Defense Forces involved, Ukraine’s Minister of Defense, the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and the General Staff, and all our weapons manufacturers for an unprecedented operation in response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure,” the Ukrainian leader noted. “Today, everyone can see the consequences for the main military crossing from Russian territory into our Ukrainian Crimea.”

“This is the result of the seventh stage of an operation carried out over several weeks, developed and coordinated by the Security Service of Ukraine together with the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine,” Zelensky added. “Our…
items.t: What We Know About Ukraine’s Strikes That Cut Russia’s Kerch Bridge Road Vehicle Span

items.title: Marine Corps removes head of specialized training unit at Twentynine Palms
items.summary:
The Marine Corps this month removed the head of its specialized training unit, a California-based group responsible for designing and managing high-level combat readiness exercises. 

Senior officials removed Col. Eric Meador from his role as director of the Tactical Training and Exercise Control Group on Nov. 9, the service told Military Times on Monday.

The Marine Corps declined to provide additional information on the reason for his removal. 

“Due to the administrative nature of this action, no further information will be provided,” Capt. Johnathon Huizar, a spokesman for the Marine Air Ground Force Training Command, said in an email.

According to the service record provided by the Marine Corps, Meador enlisted before becoming an officer in 1999. His awards include a Bronze Star and campaign meadals from Iraq and Afghanistan, among others. 

The Tactical Training and Exercise Control Group , located at Twentynine Palms, is charged with creating situations to simulate the evolving nature of combat. Founded on lessons from the Vietnam War, the organization was created in 1979 to train troops in combined arms operations.
items.t: Marine Corps removes head of specialized training unit at Twentynine Palms

items.title: Navy’s holistic health program expands to 10 bases amid broader military fitness overhaul
items.summary:
Amid a physical fitness reform effort across the military, the Navy is expanding a wellness program meant to help sailors live healthier through access to nutrition, strength, and mindfulness coaches.

The Human Performance Optimization program (HPO) launched in February at Naval Base San Diego. Rather than focus on twice-a-year fitness tests , HPO aims to help sailors build tailored, holistic fitness habits so they can stay in shape both on shore and at sea.

After a nine-month pilot program, the Navy announced on Monday that it is expanding HPO to nine more Navy bases around the world over the next 12 months. The new bases are:

Naval Station Norfolk, Virginia 

Naval Station Mayport, Florida 

Naval Base Kitsap, Washington 

Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam, Hawaii 

Commander Fleet Activities Yokosuka, Japan 

Naval Support Activity Naples, Italy 

Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland 

Naval Construction Battalion Center Gulfport, Mississippi; 

Naval Station Rota, Spain. 

“HPO gives sailors access to specialized expertise and science-backed resources to improve performance, prevent injuries, and build resilience,” Vice Adm. Brad Collins, head of Navy Installations Command, said in a press release . “Expanding these services is an investment in our people and the Navy’s ability to execute its mission.”

The three elements of HPO are cognition, nutrition, and strength. For the cognitive side, sports psychologists might work on mindfulness and breathing exercises with sailors, HPO assistant Kyle Morrison explained in a Navy video published Sept. 9. These include…
items.t: Navy’s holistic health program expands to 10 bases amid broader military fitness overhaul

items.title: Pentagon fails ninth straight audit despite progress in organizing finances
items.summary:
The Pentagon failed a financial audit for the ninth consecutive year, according to an inspector general report released Monday, but an official said a majority of its units passed for the first time.

Defense Department CFO Jules Hurst told Reuters an independent auditor found that financial statements for 14 of the Pentagon’s 25 standalone reporting entities passed in the 2026 fiscal year, which ended in September, up from 11 the prior year. Those entities account for 56% of the department’s assets and 86% of its liabilities.

“For the first time ever, a majority of assets from the department are on clean opinions,” Hurst said. The audits check whether financial statements are fairly presented and whether financial systems and processes are sound.

The Pentagon is a vast bureaucracy that has struggled with some 149 financial management systems, many of which are inadequate and outdated. They include technology built on 50-year-old computer code.

As the administration seeks a record $1.5 trillion in national defense spending from Congress, modernizing those systems has become a priority as the Pentagon strives to show lawmakers it can be trusted.

The Pentagon as a whole was first audited in 2018 and has consistently ​failed to pass annual audits because of its ⁠system and accounting problems. Congress gave it 10 years to pass, which falls in the fiscal year starting in October 2027.

Among the entities passing an audit for the first time in fiscal 2026 was the Pentagon’s Medicare-Eligible Retiree Health Care Fund.

To complete an audit without relying on the antiquated…
items.t: Pentagon fails ninth straight audit despite progress in organizing finances

items.title: Russia’s Prized Kerch Bridge Struck In Ukrainian Drone Onslaught (Updated)
items.summary:
The Kerch Bridge, one of Russia’s most strategically important and heavily defended pieces of infrastructure, spanning the Kerch Strait between Krasnodar Krai in Russia and the Kerch Peninsula of Crimea, has been struck again. The latest attacks came amid a massive Ukrainian overnight offensive that Moscow says involved 1,336 long-range drones.

Update: The Russian-installed head of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov reported a second attack on the bridge in less than 24 hours. 

The Russian-installed head of occupied Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed that the crossing, which includes both automotive and rail lanes, had been targeted earlier today, announcing temporary traffic restrictions while authorities assessed the situation.

items.title: First F-15EXs Arrive At Kadena Air Base In Japan, 25 Now Delivered To The USAF
items.summary:
The U.S. Air Force now has two F-15EX Eagle II fighters permanently forward-deployed at Kadena Air Base on the Japanese island of Okinawa. The 18th Wing has been awaiting the arrival of F-15EXs as replacements for its retired F-15C/D Eagles for years now. This milestone also highlights the continued expansion of the overall Air Force Eagle II fleet , which has now grown to 25 jets.

The 18th Wing announced that its first F-15EXs had touched down at Kadena yesterday. Prime contractor Boeing confirmed today that those jets were the 22nd and 23rd Eagle IIs produced (EX22 and EX23) in posts across its social media accounts. The expectation is that 36 F-15EXs will eventually be based in Japan, with 18 each assigned to the 44th and 67th Fighter Squadrons. 

An F-15EX Eagle II seen about to land at Kadena Air Base on November 15, 2026. USAF 

Boeing also confirmed to TWZ directly today that 25 F-15EXs have been delivered to the Air Force. This includes all of the jets in the first and second production lots. Lot 3 deliveries are now underway. The total Air Force Eagle IIs fleet is now set to reach 267 airframes, roughly double what the program of record was in 2025. 

EX22, the first Japan-bound Eagle II, had left Boeing’s plant in St. Louis in September and traveled first to Portland Air National Guard Base in Oregon. The base is collocated with Portland International Airport and is home to the Oregon Air National Guard’s 142nd Wing, the first unit to fly combat-coded F-15EXs. The 142nd has been central to coordinating and preparing the way for the deployment of Eagle IIs to…
items.t: First F-15EXs Arrive At Kadena Air Base In Japan, 25 Now Delivered To The USAF

items.title: Air Force bets on hybrid-electric aircraft for transport
items.summary:
The Air Force is pitching in nearly $5 million to help a Virginia-based aerospace company bring a 9-seat hybrid-electric airplane to flight—and to evaluate its potential use in combat.

A $4.7 million other transaction agreement contract from AFWERX will help Electra develop its EL9 prototype aircraft, building on the company’s existing EL2 two-seat prototype.

The EL9 is a small aircraft, comparable to a Cessna Caravan or Pilatus PC-12. Its size, combined with the ability to take off and land in just 150 feet, could make it good to use for special operations. 

“The USAF has always been interested in what new technology can bring to the battlefield, and the new contract will let it test what an ultra-[short take off and landing] aircraft can do in service,” said Douglas Royce, senior aerospace and power systems analyst for Forecast International. “The contract isn’t a signal that the USAF is ready to acquire this type of aircraft, but the vulnerability of traditional air bases to missile attack may encourage the use of distributed operations in combat zones. Operating an ultra-STOL platform from short or improvised runways may be a part of that concept.”

“The special forces use would make sense because having a…
items.t: Air Force bets on hybrid-electric aircraft for transport

items.title: First permanently assigned F-15EXs touch down at Kadena Air Base
items.summary:
A Japan air base became the first American installation abroad to receive two permanently assigned F-15EX Eagle IIs and the second-ever Air Force location to field the fighter jet . 

Kadena Air Base , located in Okinawa, Japan, received two of the fighter aircraft Sunday as the Air Force strives to increase U.S. airpower in the Pacific, according to a recent service release , especially as the base continues to replace its F-15C/D fleet.

“[F-15EXs] strengthen our ability to deter aggression, respond to emerging threats and defend Japan alongside our allies and partners,” 18th Wing Commander Brig. Gen. John Gallemore said in the release.

“Their permanent presence at Kadena reinforces our commitment to the U.S.-Japan alliance and ensures we continue to bring advanced combat capabilities to one of the most strategically important regions in the world,” he continued.

In November 2022, the base first began withdrawing its legacy F-15C/D aircraft after four decades of service. The transition included rotational deployments of fourth- and fifth-generation fighters to maintain a fighter presence while maintainers, operators and mission support airmen sought the expertise needed to utilize a new platform as soon as it reaches operational capability, the release says.

Two years after the Oregon Air National Guard received theirs, the F-15EXs at Kadena are expected to increase the base’s ability to conduct counterair operations and boost the service’s forward-deployed capabilities.

With advanced avionics, modernized electronic warfare systems and heightened weapons-carrying…
items.t: First permanently assigned F-15EXs touch down at Kadena Air Base

items.title: DoD restores parental access to teens’ medical records
items.summary:
Military parents will be able to view their teenagers’ Defense Department electronic health records more easily starting Wednesday — a change parents have said is necessary to guide health decisions for their children. 

Beginning Nov. 18, dependent children ages 13-18 will be able to go into the MHS Genesis portal and grant permission for their parents to view their medical records. Previously, parents had to go into patient administration offices at their military hospital or clinic and have their teenage children sign a consent form for parents to have access. 

The cumbersome process and restrictions, which went into effect in 2023 , have vexed military parents, according to Army Surgeon General Lt. Gen. Mary Izaguirre. 

“The parents don’t have access to [records] based on the current departmental policy, and then the children don’t have ID cards to sign in to get into [the Defense Enrollment and Eligibility Records System] … so there’s this space,” Izaguirre said Oct. 13 during a forum for families at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting. 

Parental access to minor medical records largely depends on state and federal regulations. An update in 2023 to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act’s (HIPAA) privacy rules modified the circumstances under which a person’s health information can be disclosed under federal law. 

The change, which followed the Supreme Court’s decision in 2022 to overturn Roe v. Wade, prohibited doctors, insurance companies and other health organizations from disclosing patient information to state officials for…
items.t: DoD restores parental access to teens’ medical records

items.title: U.S. Army Now Wants Concrete Bunkers For Troops In Israel, Saudi Arabia And Lebanon
items.summary:
In order to better protect personnel, U.S. Army Central (ARCENT) is looking to replace converted shipping containers with concrete bunkers as shelters at several locations in Israel, Lebanon and Saudi Arabia. The effort underscores questions about why more investments in physical hardening were not made in the region well before the current conflict. 

The Army’s search for companies that can build the new bunkers also came just days before 60 Minutes had interviews with family members of troops killed in Kuwait and a soldier who was there raising concerns about why more was not done to provide even basic hardening at a base where six soldiers died in an Iranian drone attack. Iranian attacks across the region also destroyed and damaged aircraft , radars and other equipment, and did billions in damage to infrastructure used by the U.S. military.

For years now , TWZ has been highlighting how the lack of hardened infrastructure at American military facilities abroad and at home creates worrisome vulnerabilities .

“Due to elevated regional force protection conditions, there is an urgent, high-priority requirement to replace non-standard personnel protection shelters (e.g., converted shipping containers) and provide standardized precast reinforced concrete Indirect Fire (IDF) bunkers,” according to a sources sought synopsis posted Nov. 13 on the U.S. government’s main online contracting portal. “The objective is to safeguard U.S. and Coalition service members operating in potentially hostile environments across multiple countries in the USCENTCOM [U.S. Central Command] Area…
items.t: U.S. Army Now Wants Concrete Bunkers For Troops In Israel, Saudi Arabia And Lebanon

items.title: Air Force training chief’s No. 1 priority: Be more like the Marines
items.summary:
The three-star general overseeing training for the Air Force and Space Force said Monday that he’s serious about getting newly trained airmen to emulate the culture of another service: the Marine Corps.

In a wide-ranging discussion hosted by The Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, Lt. Gen. Clark Quinn called an identity shift his top command priority.

“If you find a Marine, where they’re active-duty, retired, doesn’t matter, and you ask them, ‘Hey, what do you do?’ Their answer is, ‘I’m a Marine,'” Quinn said. If you ask the same of an airman, he added, you’re more likely to hear him or her identify by their specific career field. 

“Part of what we are trying to do in forging airmen is to get that fundamental underpinning that is, what does it mean to be an airman,” he said. “I don’t know that by the end of my time here, an airman is going to go, ‘I’m an airman,’ but that’s the mentality that we’re trying to drive into it.”

The Air Force has been emphasizing its cultural identity – what service members sometimes call “airmindedness” – in other ways. A Basic Military Training overhaul currently underway gives the most junior trainees the opportunity, for example, to load and rearm an F-16 Fighting Falcon, emphasizing every airman’s role in providing airpower to the joint force.

In a September interview, officers leading that effort told Military Times that the added intensity and hands-on learning was making trainees more curious about combat scenarios and prompting them to think critically and independently about their training.

While it’s not a further effort…
items.t: Air Force training chief’s No. 1 priority: be more like the Marines

items.title: New Bow Sonar Dome For Heavily Damaged Submarine USS Connecticut Seen For The First Time (Updated)
items.summary:
TWZ has obtained new details about the ongoing repairs to the Seawolf class submarine USS Connecticut following collision with an underwater seamount in the South China Sea in 2021. The Navy had been looking at a roughly three-year timeline for the construction of a replacement bow sonar dome. In the end, it took just under a year for it to be built. The overall schedule for repairs to Connecticut has suffered delays, and we were the first to report that the boat is now not expected to return to service until next summer.

Editor’s note: After this story was published, Janicki Industries reached out to us to ask that the image of the dome be taken down while an additional review is conducted. Out of courtesy, we agreed, and we will repost it if and when it is fully approved. 

Janicki Industries produced the new bow sonar dome in approximately 10 months and delivered it to the Navy in 2024, the company told us today. Janicki has a history of producing “sonar domes and precision machined hardware” for U.S. nuclear submarine programs, according to its website . It has also supported various high-profile aerospace programs, including the B-21 Raider bomber and F-35 Joint Strike Fighter . 

Connecticut ’s bow had initially remained attached, at least to some degree, following the collision five years ago, according to a heavily redacted Navy report on the accident . However, the entire bow structure subsequently broke away as the submarine limped to Guam . The boat then sailed to San Diego, California , and then to the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard & Intermediate Maintenance…
items.t: New Bow Sonar Dome For Heavily Damaged Submarine USS Connecticut Seen For The First Time

items.title: Army lieutenant colonel arrested in UK over allegedly spying for Russia may face US charges
items.summary:
An Army lieutenant colonel attached to a NATO headquarters in England is suspected of spying for Russia. The soldier was originally arrested in the United Kingdom, where it was expected he would face an indictment over the alleged national security breach, but now he may face espionage charges in the United States, an Army official said. 

The Army announced that a senior officer was arrested Nov. 10 near Gloucester, England. Media outlets reported, and Task & Purpose confirmed, that the soldier involved is Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, 41, who was assigned to NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps headquarters. The headquarters is a British-led unit with 20 countries assigned to it.

Army officials said Tyner was arrested on suspicion of violating sections of the U.K.’s National Security Act of 2023 for obtaining, copying, recording or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.

News 

Navy relieves commander of destroyer USS Michael Murphy 

By David Roza , Nicholas Slayton 

News 

Entire command team of USS South Dakota relieved following grounding incident 

By Nicholas Slayton 

News 

Marine Corps relieves Tactical Training Exercise Control Group commander without explanation 

By Nicholas Slayton

In late August, President Donald Trump announced what he called the “biggest oil deal in world history.” Since then, the full text of the accord — which grants the U.S. sweeping access to Venezuela’s oil reserves — has been one of the most sought-after secrets in Washington, D.C.

Troops living in barracks with “emergency conditions” that pose health or safety risks can get temporary lodging on or off base, according to new rules set by the Pentagon. 

In a Nov. 10 memo, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth directed the services to follow barracks standards laid out in October by the Assistant Secretary of War for Energy, Installations, and Environment, Mark Dale . The new guidelines classify barracks maintenance work orders into three categories: emergency, urgent and routine. 

The memo did not provide specific examples of what scenarios would classify under the three categories. Barracks have become a highly scrutinized quality-of-life issue in recent years, with troops facing problems that range from mold and pest infestations impacting their health to serious safety concerns as well as more routine nuisances like broken air conditioners in hot climates and delayed maintenance on aging buildings .

The military services were told to inspect barracks by Monday and take actions to address “emergency conditions” within 24 hours, which includes providing troops with temporary quarters if their room isn’t “safe” enough to live in.

Rob Evans, founder of the barracks review app, Hots&Cots , and an advocate for junior enlisted housing, said the urgency behind these instructions is right, but “service members have been through this before.”

items.title: Navy relieves commander of destroyer USS Michael Murphy
items.summary:
The Navy quietly relieved Cmdr. Caitlin Cunningham, skipper of the guided-missile destroyer USS Michael Murphy, on Sept. 27 “due to a loss of confidence to command,” a Navy official told Task & Purpose.

The relief came nine months into the ship’s 11-month deployment to the Middle East, where the USS Michael Murphy helped enforce a naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, escort tankers, launch Tomahawk cruise missiles, and defend against Iranian drone and missile attacks. The USS Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group, which the Murphy was a part of, was later awarded the Presidential Unit Citation. 

USNI News first reported on Cunningham’s removal .

No reason was given for Cunningham’s firing. The Navy regularly uses the term “loss of confidence” as a catchall for the many reasons a commander can be relieved. The term is used for everything from mishaps onboard the vessel to personal misconduct by an officer. 

Cmdr. David Nicholas has helmed the destroyer since Cunningham was relieved.

Both are reportedly longer than any previous destroyer cruise since World War II. However, the record may not hold for long, as USS John Finn is on pace to surpass both.

Spruance pulled out of Naval Base San Diego on November 21, 2025, alongside Nimitz class aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln , on what the crews expected would be a routine deployment to the Western Pacific. Murphy linked up with the strike group 10 days later as it sailed past her homeport at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam, Hawaii.

Both ships, which endured conditions just as grueling as Lincoln , if not more so, returned to their homeports over the past 24 hours. Joe Courtney (D-Conn.), the ranking member of the House Seapower and Projection Forces Subcommittee, and Adam Smith (D-Wash.), the ranking member of the House Armed Services Committee, cites The Day’s reporting and says the committee had not been informed for nearly a month, which they called “unacceptable.”

“In the wake of the collisions affecting USS Fitzgerald (DDG 62), USS John S. McCain (DDG 56), and the grounding incidents involving USS Hartford (SSN 768) and USS Connecticut (SSN 22), clear and timely communication with Congress was necessary to make informed decisions to ensure personnel safety and readiness of the fleet,” Courtney and Smith wrote.

items.title: Defense Business Brief: This Ukraine-founded drone maker is now worth $6 billion. What now?
items.summary:
Build more, faster—and then integrate it all together. That was the gist of my conversation with  Oleg Rogynskyy, CEO of Ukraine-founded drone company UFORCE, that’s now valued at more than $6 billion after landing a $700 million series A funding round this week. 

“Our m.o. is to go to exercises and actually do stuff,” Rogynskyy said via video conference while at a defense conference in Oslo, Norway. “The unmanned surface vessels have had a massive impact on the Black Sea fleet. That has been public and recorded. Our Nemesis UAV platform has destroyed over 10,000 Russian vehicles. We know we shine the best when we are in real operations.”

And now with “a very deliberately designed funding round” complete, the next move is to become ubiquitous. 

It “supports our mission to help Ukraine defend itself, but also bring out these platforms…that have been so effective in making defense operations so much cheaper and so much more effective in Ukraine to help the rest of the democratic world defend itself and prevent a future war,” he said.

items.title: The Air Force’s Newest Trainer Is An Aerobatic Plane
items.summary:
The U.S. Air Force unveiled its newest aircraft today by flying them over the Air Force Academy , where they will be used to train a future generation of pilots and serve as the basis for a new aerial demonstration team. The goal is to give cadets a chance to experience high g-force flying while also providing a new recruiting tool to boost the flagging ranks of Air Force pilots .

Dubbed the T-19A Kestrel, the aircraft are two-seat, single-engine GB1 Gamebird all-carbon-fiber aerial performance planes. They were made by Game Aerospace Composites , a Bentonville, Arkansas, company that describes these planes as “the ultimate aerobatic aircraft for pilots seeking an exhilarating flying experience.”

The Air Force has received four of these planes.

T-19A Kestrels lining up for flight at the U.S. Air Force Academy in Colorado Springs, Colorado. (U.S. Air Force courtesy photo) 

A Boost For Pilot Training 

The flight over the Cadet Wing’s noon meal formation “marks the formal arrival of the Academy’s first powered aerobatic aircraft, which recently completed its final military certification flights,” the Air Force noted in a release Thursday afternoon.

The T-19As “will enhance the Academy’s elite airmanship program,” the Air Force added. “By partnering with world-class civilian aerobatic pilots and curriculum developers, the Academy aims to field a nationally competitive aerobatic and demonstration team.”

The Air Force’s top general called the T-19A program “historic.”

“Going from an idea to four aircraft built and delivered in 10 months is unprecedented and a testament…
items.t: The Air Force’s Newest Trainer Is An Aerobatic Plane

items.title: Second world war ‘brain’ bunker in cliffs of Dover opens to public
items.summary:
Hidden bunker, entered via a hatch in a field, controlled a gun battery used to attack German ships in Channel

It has been kept secret for decades, buried four metres deep into the white cliffs of Dover. But from Friday, members of the public will finally be able to visit a pioneering command bunker that was ordered by Winston Churchill and proved a vital defence during the second world war.

The Fan Bay plotting room, which is encased in concrete, housed the first land-based computer-aided targeting system. This acted as a “brain” for a gun battery that was used to defend Dover and attack German ships in the Channel, according to Jon Barker, who led the excavation project for the National Trust.

items.t: Second world war ‘brain’ bunker in cliffs of Dover opens to public

items.title: High-Speed Aircraft Startup Hermeus Joins Forces With Northrop Grumman
items.summary:
Aviation startup Hermeus and established prime contractor Northrop Grumman say they are now working together toward the aim of delivering operational uncrewed aircraft capable of high-supersonic, if not hypersonic , flight to the U.S. military. Through a newly announced partnership, Northrop Grumman is set to integrate electronic warfare systems, sensors, autonomy packages, and other capabilities onto “next-generation” Hermeus drones.

Hermeus and Northrop Grumman announced their team-up earlier today. Hermeus, which was founded in 2018, has already flown a succession of ever-more capable uncrewed jet-powered Quarterhorse demonstrator drones . The delta-winged Quarterhorse Mk 2.1 was the first of these to break the sound barrier during a test flight in May. The company is now working on a further evolved Quarterhorse Mk 2.2, which it hopes to push beyond Mach 2. 

A look at the progression in Hermeus Quarterhorse drone designs to date, starting with the non-flying Mk 0 ‘iron bird’ test rig on the far left. Hermeus 

Hermeus’ stated end goal is a design capable of hypersonic flight. The company has also previously shown renderings of a planned “mission plane” prototype described as being capable of “high-Mach” flight and equipped with six underwing pylons, three under each wing, as well as one along the centerline.

A rendering of Hermeus’ planned “mission plane.” Hermeus 

Quarterhorse Mk 2.1 has already demonstrated the ability to release stores at high speed. In September, Hermeus also unveiled Ramjet-X , a smaller ramjet-powered platform that can be air-launched from…
items.t: High-Speed Aircraft Startup Hermeus Joins Forces With Northrop Grumman

items.title: A natural-gas project off Alaska may be a Russian ploy
items.summary:
This story was originally published by ProPublica.

To an outsider, the research boats bobbing in the frigid and stormy Beaufort Sea off Alaska would seem little cause for alarm. Oil and gas companies have regularly explored the area for decades. 

For this project, businessmen from the United Arab Emirates were touting a plan to tap the vast natural gas reserves that lay beneath the tundra of Alaska’s North Slope. They promised the operation would eventually be American-owned. No one could dispute Alaska’s dire energy needs — not to mention the potential for lucrative exports. 

The surveyors last year used specialized equipment to map the depth and shape of the seabed, collect samples of shallow marine sediments and conduct sonar scans to check for obstructions such as shipwrecks. Documents show that their work was not far, as the crow flies, from the start of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline System — a cornerstone of U.S. energy production. An Air Force long-range radar station sat just to the west. More than 100 miles off the coast, the Navy’s fast-attack nuclear submarines sometimes practiced surfacing through the thick Arctic ice.

But this project was far from routine. While the contractors performing the work were American, the UAE company paying for the surveys was actually being steered by Russia’s…
items.t: A natural-gas project off Alaska may be a Russian ploy

items.title: Ukraine Says Starshield Disruptions Are Back As U.S. Negotiators Meet With Putin
items.summary:
For the second time in a month , Ukrainian officials and military personnel are complaining that weapons using SpaceX’s vital Starshield satellite communications system have had limits placed on the speeds at which they can operate. The officials say the latest Starshield issues are impairing Ukraine’s ability to defend against Russian missile barrages and strike targets far behind the lines in Ukrainian territory that Russia holds. Ukrainians made similar claims in October, and the service was eventually restored .

The complaints, from President Volodymyr Zelensky, one of his main advisors, and frontline troops, are being made as U.S. negotiators met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in another White House-brokered effort to end the war. Some Ukrainians are reportedly even claiming the Starshield system is being impacted to pressure Ukraine to bend to Russian demands to give up territory. 

SpaceX denied the allegations.

“This is false,” a SpaceX official told us. “There has been no change.”

A Ukrainian soldier of the 61st Separate Mechanized Brigade uses the Starlink system. (Photo by Maxym Marusenko/NurPhoto via Getty Images) NurPhoto 

While TWZ cannot independently verify the Ukrainian claims about Starshield, the issue again highlights the challenges Kyiv faces fighting a war while relying on donated equipment and services. The country is working on alternatives, including developing its own satellite communications system . However, even Ukrainian officials acknowledge that it won’t come close to replacing the SpaceX system.

items.title: GOP tries to speed-walk search for GAO's next chief
items.summary:
A lame-duck Congress is suddenly hastening the process to find a new long-term leader of a governmentwide watchdog agency that has drawn the ire of the Trump administration. 

House and Senate Republicans faced calls over the past two years to start the bipartisan process of interviewing candidates to lead the Government Accountability Office. 

Under the current process, the selection of the GAO comptroller general begins with a commission of 10 senior House and Senate lawmakers from both parties that recommends individuals for the position to the president. 

Whoever the president selects is subject to Senate confirmation for one nonrenewable 15-year term. The last time lawmakers vetted candidates for GAO’s top job in 2010, the congressional commission spent more than a year on its search. 

This time around, members of the commission are being given a single day to come up with candidate recommendations, after receiving notice on Veterans Day. The commission is meant to recommend at least three candidates for the job.

items.t: GOP tries to speed-walk search for GAO's next chief

items.title: Vets groups slam House for quietly passing divisive benefits bill on Veterans Day
items.summary:
A divisive bill that cuts disability benefits for veterans with sleep apnea and tinnitus while simultaneously granting compensation for combat veterans was passed by the House on Veterans Day — evoking condemnation from Democrats and veterans groups.

The Take Care of America’s Veterans Act is a large legislative package with dozens of bills, including a controversial set of policies that drew strong opposition from the start. Veteran Service Organizations said that the package would cut disability benefits from one group — veterans with sleep apnea and tinnitus ratings — and act as an “offset” to pay for another group, combat wounded veterans.

Democrats and veteran advocates criticized House Republicans for passing disability cuts on Veterans Day — and doing so with a voice vote where members call out “aye” or “no” the loudest, instead of recording an official vote under their name. 

“On a day when America honors the brave men and women who stepped forward to defend our freedom, House leaders chose to sneak through legislation threatening earned benefits for millions of veterans, their families and survivors,” Disabled American Veterans National Commander John Donovan said in a statement. “Veterans risked their lives to guarantee our right to vote, and those who have the privilege of serving in Congress should have the backbone and decency to openly stand behind their votes, not hide like thieves in the night.”

Republicans declared the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act passage a “historic healthcare and benefits expansion,” noting that the bill gets rid of limits for…
items.t: Vets groups slam House for quietly passing divisive benefits bill on Veterans Day

items.title: L-39NG Skyfox Jets Could Give Ukraine A Critical New Russian Drone Hunting Capability
items.summary:
The Czech Republic could supply Ukraine with up to 16 Aero L-39NG Skyfox aircraft, potentially giving Kyiv another option for countering Russia’s Shahed-type attack drones . The proposal includes four aircraft previously agreed to for transfer and 12 more that Czech officials are now discussing with their Ukrainian counterparts.

Czech Deputy Prime Minister and Industry and Trade Minister Karel Havlíček raised the expanded arrangement during a visit to Kyiv yesterday, where he met Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi. Havlíček described the discussions as encouraging but did not announce a finalized agreement for the additional aircraft.

L-39NG Skyfox. Aero Vodochody 

Skyfox is based on the Cold War-era Aero L-39 Albatros jet trainer, a rugged and reliable Soviet aircraft that was produced in the thousands and served all over the globe. The new L-39NG was reworked and modernized in the 2010s in an effort to recapture jet trainer market share that had waned as the Soviet design was increasingly passed over for more modern alternatives. Many L-39s are also flown privately in the United States and are used for contracted air support services for the U.S. military. One of the firms that uses them, Draken International , actually assisted in the L-39NG project and acted as a U.S. anchor for the program.

The Skyfox’s redesigned structure makes use of modern materials, reducing weight and increasing structural lifespan to 15,000 flight hours. The American Williams FJ44-4M turbofan, a very widely used jet engine that is found on many private jets, replaces the original…
items.t: L-39NG Skyfox Jets Could Give Ukraine A Critical New Russian Drone Hunting Capability
